thread.title: Childhood Trauma May Up Risk for Reincarceration

title: Childhood Trauma May Up Risk for Reincarceration
text:
Childhood Trauma May Up Risk for Reincarceration Adverse childhood events included parental absence, parental suicide MedpageToday by Elizabeth Hlavinka, Staff Writer, MedPage Today October 27, 2018
AUSTIN, Texas -- Patients with adverse childhood events (ACE) were more likely to be reincarcerated, according to preliminary results of a retrospective study.
While 61% of reincarcerated men have reported experiencing ACEs in past literature, the current review showed that 96% of men with mental health symptoms, such as post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), depression, and suicidality, experienced past trauma, reported Mansfield Mela, MBBS, of the University of Saskatchewan in Canada.
And the number of ACEs increased with recidivism rates, with patients with at least seven ACEs reporting an average 28.8 previous convictions and 24.08 non-violent convictions, followed by patients with 4-6 ACEs and 0-3 ACEs, Mela said at the American Academy of Psychiatry and the Law (AAPL) annual meeting.
Specifically, patients who suffered parental deficits in childhood, including the absence, incarceration, or suicidal death of a parent, were more likely to be reincarcerated ( P =0.004), he reported.
"The data show that if you report more than four ACEs, we need to target specific, trauma-informed care your way," Mela told MedPage Today. "Instead of approaching this from policy down, this individual should be selected and [taught] how to manage [his] anger."
Previous studies have demonstrated that childhood trauma can increase the risk for psychosis , anxiety, PTSD, or an increased chance of developing substance abuse. Additionally, trauma can be "inherited" by a child from his parents, Mela said. Some studies have demonstrated that children who experience ACEs had higher levels of criminal thinking . Another study reported that nearly three-fourths of prisoners presented PTSD symptoms and 30.7% were at risk of re-offending.
The current retrospective study observed patients at the Regional Psychiatric Centre in Saskatoon, Canada, a multi-level secure treatment facility (MOU), from 1996 to 2006. In total, 200 patients were included for analysis, and 80 were included in this preliminary presentation. All of the participants were male, about half were single, and the average age was 33. Inmates had an average sentence length of 5 years, and had re-entered the community for a mean 13 years before being reincarcerated.
The majority of patients reported experiencing parenting deficit (65), while 54 reported physical trauma, and 29 sexual trauma. On average, patients reported five total ACEs.
Individuals were reincarcerated more often if they were younger ( P =0.024) or had more convictions before admission ( P= 0.044), specifically non-violent convictions ( P= 0.027), Mela said.
Mela stated that standard practice is missing a trauma-informed treatment model for these highly complex patients. And while primary intervention mechanisms should begin in childhood, inmates that are convicted should be thoroughly evaluated for ACEs, so that their past trauma may be taken into account when developing a treatment plan.
"The prison is a different world, divided very strictly by this boundary, and we keep prisoners there with no connection," Mela said. "There has been evidence that if you connect someone in prison with someone in the community, it provides normalization, socialization, and more importantly, causes a turning point. If you can get this adult who had been traumatized...connected with their own family, distant family, or another family, they begin to see why its important to be more social."
Mela disclosed no relevant relationships with industry. 2018-10-27T18:00:00-0400 Primary Source American Academy of Psychiatry and the Law
